package com.fitt.workouts.service;

import com.fitt.workouts.domain.MuscleGroup;
import com.fitt.workouts.dto.AddExerciseEntryRequest;
import com.fitt.workouts.dto.CreateWorkoutSessionRequest;
import com.fitt.workouts.dto.ExerciseEntryResponse;
import com.fitt.workouts.dto.ExerciseResponse;
import com.fitt.workouts.dto.LogSetRequest;
import com.fitt.workouts.dto.SetEntryResponse;
import com.fitt.workouts.dto.WorkoutSessionResponse;
import com.fitt.workouts.persistence.entity.ExerciseEntryEntity;
import com.fitt.workouts.persistence.entity.ExerciseEntity;
import com.fitt.workouts.persistence.entity.SetEntryEntity;
import com.fitt.workouts.persistence.entity.WorkoutSessionEntity;
import com.fitt.workouts.repository.ExerciseEntryRepository;
import com.fitt.workouts.repository.ExerciseRepository;
import com.fitt.workouts.repository.SetEntryRepository;
import com.fitt.workouts.repository.WorkoutSessionRepository;
import com.fitt.workouts.service.exception.ExerciseNotFoundException;
import com.fitt.workouts.service.exception.WorkoutSessionNotFoundException;
import org.springframework.security.access.AccessDeniedException;
import org.springframework.stereotype.Service;
import org.springframework.transaction.annotation.Transactional;

import java.time.Instant;
import java.util.List;

@Service
@Transactional(readOnly = true)
public class WorkoutSessionServiceImpl implements WorkoutSessionService {

    private final WorkoutSessionRepository sessionRepository;
    private final ExerciseEntryRepository entryRepository;
    private final SetEntryRepository setEntryRepository;
    private final ExerciseRepository exerciseRepository;

    public WorkoutSessionServiceImpl(
            WorkoutSessionRepository sessionRepository,
            ExerciseEntryRepository entryRepository,
            SetEntryRepository setEntryRepository,
            ExerciseRepository exerciseRepository) {
        this.sessionRepository = sessionRepository;
        this.entryRepository = entryRepository;
        this.setEntryRepository = setEntryRepository;
        this.exerciseRepository = exerciseRepository;
    }

    @Override
    @Transactional
    public WorkoutSessionResponse createSession(Long ownerUserId, CreateWorkoutSessionRequest request) {
        WorkoutSessionEntity session = new WorkoutSessionEntity();
        session.setOwnerUserId(ownerUserId);
        session.setStartedAt(request.startedAt());
        session.setWorkoutPlanDayId(request.workoutPlanDayId());
        session.setNotes(request.notes());

        return toResponse(sessionRepository.save(session));
    }

    @Override
    public List<WorkoutSessionResponse> listSessions(Long ownerUserId) {
        return sessionRepository.findByOwnerUserIdOrderByStartedAtDesc(ownerUserId)
                .stream()
                .map(this::toResponse)
                .toList();
    }

    @Override
    public WorkoutSessionResponse getSession(Long ownerUserId, Long sessionId) {
        WorkoutSessionEntity session = loadAndVerifyOwnership(ownerUserId, sessionId);
        return toResponse(session);
    }

    @Override
    @Transactional
    public WorkoutSessionResponse finishSession(Long ownerUserId, Long sessionId) {
        WorkoutSessionEntity session = loadAndVerifyOwnership(ownerUserId, sessionId);
        session.setFinishedAt(Instant.now());
        return toResponse(sessionRepository.save(session));
    }

    @Override
    @Transactional
    public void deleteSession(Long ownerUserId, Long sessionId) {
        WorkoutSessionEntity session = loadAndVerifyOwnership(ownerUserId, sessionId);
        sessionRepository.delete(session);
    }

    @Override
    @Transactional
    public WorkoutSessionResponse addExerciseEntry(Long ownerUserId, Long sessionId, AddExerciseEntryRequest request) {
        WorkoutSessionEntity session = loadAndVerifyOwnership(ownerUserId, sessionId);

        ExerciseEntity exercise = exerciseRepository.findById(request.exerciseId())
                .orElseThrow(() -> new ExerciseNotFoundException(request.exerciseId()));

        // append to the end of whatever is already in this session
        int nextIndex = session.getExerciseEntries().size();

        ExerciseEntryEntity entry = new ExerciseEntryEntity();
        entry.setOrderIndex(nextIndex);
        // session.addExerciseEntry() keeps both sides of the relationship in sync
        session.addExerciseEntry(entry, exercise);

        return toResponse(sessionRepository.save(session));
    }

    @Override
    @Transactional
    public WorkoutSessionResponse removeExerciseEntry(Long ownerUserId, Long sessionId, Long entryId) {
        WorkoutSessionEntity session = loadAndVerifyOwnership(ownerUserId, sessionId);

        ExerciseEntryEntity target = session.getExerciseEntries()
                .stream()
                .filter(e -> e.getId().equals(entryId))
                .findFirst()
                .orElseThrow(() -> new IllegalArgumentException("Exercise entry not found in this session"));

        // orphanRemoval on the parent takes care of the DELETE
        session.removeExerciseEntry(target);

        return toResponse(sessionRepository.save(session));
    }

    @Override
    @Transactional
    public WorkoutSessionResponse logSet(Long ownerUserId, Long sessionId, Long entryId, LogSetRequest request) {
        WorkoutSessionEntity session = loadAndVerifyOwnership(ownerUserId, sessionId);

        ExerciseEntryEntity entry = session.getExerciseEntries()
                .stream()
                .filter(e -> e.getId().equals(entryId))
                .findFirst()
                .orElseThrow(() -> new IllegalArgumentException("Exercise entry not found in this session"));

        int nextSetNumber = entry.getSetEntries().size() + 1;

        SetEntryEntity set = new SetEntryEntity();
        set.setSetNumber(nextSetNumber);
        set.setReps(request.reps());
        set.setWeightKg(request.weightKg());
        set.setRpe(request.rpe());
        set.setCompletedAt(Instant.now());
        // entry.addSetEntry() syncs both sides
        entry.addSetEntry(set);

        return toResponse(sessionRepository.save(session));
    }

    @Override
    @Transactional
    public WorkoutSessionResponse deleteSet(Long ownerUserId, Long sessionId, Long entryId, Long setId) {
        WorkoutSessionEntity session = loadAndVerifyOwnership(ownerUserId, sessionId);

        ExerciseEntryEntity entry = session.getExerciseEntries()
                .stream()
                .filter(e -> e.getId().equals(entryId))
                .findFirst()
                .orElseThrow(() -> new IllegalArgumentException("Exercise entry not found in this session"));

        SetEntryEntity target = entry.getSetEntries()
                .stream()
                .filter(s -> s.getId().equals(setId))
                .findFirst()
                .orElseThrow(() -> new IllegalArgumentException("Set not found in this exercise entry"));

        entry.removeSetEntry(target);

        return toResponse(sessionRepository.save(session));
    }

    // load and verify ownership in one shot
    // every operation goes through this before doing anything
    private WorkoutSessionEntity loadAndVerifyOwnership(Long ownerUserId, Long sessionId) {
        WorkoutSessionEntity session = sessionRepository.findById(sessionId)
                .orElseThrow(() -> new WorkoutSessionNotFoundException(sessionId));

        if (!ownerUserId.equals(session.getOwnerUserId())) {
            throw new AccessDeniedException("You do not own this session");
        }

        return session;
    }

    private WorkoutSessionResponse toResponse(WorkoutSessionEntity entity) {
        List<ExerciseEntryResponse> entries = entity.getExerciseEntries()
                .stream()
                .map(this::toEntryResponse)
                .toList();

        return new WorkoutSessionResponse(
                entity.getId(),
                entity.getOwnerUserId(),
                entity.getWorkoutPlanDayId(),
                entity.getStartedAt(),
                entity.getFinishedAt(),
                entity.getNotes(),
                entity.getCreatedAt(),
                entries
        );
    }

    private ExerciseEntryResponse toEntryResponse(ExerciseEntryEntity entity) {
        List<SetEntryResponse> sets = entity.getSetEntries()
                .stream()
                .map(this::toSetResponse)
                .toList();

        ExerciseResponse exercise = new ExerciseResponse(
                entity.getExercise().getId(),
                entity.getExercise().getName(),
                MuscleGroup.valueOf(entity.getExercise().getMuscleGroup()),
                entity.getExercise().isCustom()
        );

        return new ExerciseEntryResponse(
                entity.getId(),
                entity.getOrderIndex(),
                exercise,
                sets
        );
    }

    private SetEntryResponse toSetResponse(SetEntryEntity entity) {
        return new SetEntryResponse(
                entity.getId(),
                entity.getSetNumber(),
                entity.getReps(),
                entity.getWeightKg(),
                entity.getRpe(),
                entity.getCompletedAt()
        );
    }
}

# Getting Started

### Reference Documentation

For further reference, please consider the following sections:

* [Official Apache Maven documentation](https://maven.apache.org/guides/index.html)
* [Spring Boot Maven Plugin Reference Guide](https://docs.spring.io/spring-boot/4.0.1/maven-plugin)
* [Create an OCI image](https://docs.spring.io/spring-boot/4.0.1/maven-plugin/build-image.html)
* [Spring Data JPA](https://docs.spring.io/spring-boot/4.0.1/reference/data/sql.html#data.sql.jpa-and-spring-data)
* [Spring Security](https://docs.spring.io/spring-boot/4.0.1/reference/web/spring-security.html)
* [Validation](https://docs.spring.io/spring-boot/4.0.1/reference/io/validation.html)
* [Spring Web](https://docs.spring.io/spring-boot/4.0.1/reference/web/servlet.html)

### Guides

The following guides illustrate how to use some features concretely:

* [Accessing Data with JPA](https://spring.io/guides/gs/accessing-data-jpa/)
* [Securing a Web Application](https://spring.io/guides/gs/securing-web/)
* [Spring Boot and OAuth2](https://spring.io/guides/tutorials/spring-boot-oauth2/)
* [Authenticating a User with LDAP](https://spring.io/guides/gs/authenticating-ldap/)
* [Validation](https://spring.io/guides/gs/validating-form-input/)
* [Building a RESTful Web Service](https://spring.io/guides/gs/rest-service/)
* [Serving Web Content with Spring MVC](https://spring.io/guides/gs/serving-web-content/)
* [Building REST services with Spring](https://spring.io/guides/tutorials/rest/)

### Maven Parent overrides

Due to Maven's design, elements are inherited from the parent POM to the project POM.
While most of the inheritance is fine, it also inherits unwanted elements like `<license>` and `<developers>` from the
parent.
To prevent this, the project POM contains empty overrides for these elements.
If you manually switch to a different parent and actually want the inheritance, you need to remove those overrides.

# ADR-0001: Architecture Style for FITT

Status: Accepted  
Date: 2025-12-23

## Decision

For version 1, FITT will use a modular monolith architecture for the backend, with a separate frontend client consuming a single backend API.

The backend will be deployed as one application, but structured internally into clear modules with well-defined responsibilities and boundaries. These modules will communicate through explicit interfaces rather than shared, unrestricted access.

## Context

This project is both a learning effort and a real application I intend to use. I am working as a solo developer with limited time, budget, and infrastructure. Early complexity must be controlled while still allowing the system to grow in a clean and professional way.

The application will support a web frontend initially (Angular), with a long-term goal of adding an iOS client. Both clients should be able to rely on the same backend API without changes to business logic.

## Rationale

A modular monolith fits these constraints because it:

- Keeps deployment simple (one backend service)
- Avoids the operational and cognitive overhead of microservices
- Encourages clean separation of concerns inside the backend
- Makes future refactoring or extraction of modules possible if needed
- Is widely recommended as a starting point for systems that may grow

Separating the frontend and backend allows independent development and supports multiple client types while keeping the backend authoritative for business rules and data integrity.

## Alternatives Considered

Microservices were considered but rejected for v1 due to:
- Increased operational complexity
- Infrastructure overhead
- Higher risk of premature abstraction
- Poor fit for a solo developer at this stage

A fully monolithic backend without internal modular boundaries was also rejected, as it would make the system harder to reason about and evolve over time.

## Consequences

This decision means:
- The backend will enforce boundaries through package structure and design
- Architectural discipline is required to prevent cross-module coupling
- Scaling will focus on code organization and clarity, not service proliferation
- Future extraction into separate services remains possible but is not required

This architecture supports learning, maintainability, and future growth without unnecessary complexity.

# ADR-0002: Backend Domain Modules for FITT

Status: Accepted  
Date: 2025-12-23

## Decision

For version 1, the FITT backend will be structured as a modular monolith with the following core domain modules:

- Identity
- Workouts
- Measurements
- Nutrition

Each module owns its data, rules, and persistence. Modules communicate through explicit service boundaries rather than shared, unrestricted access.

## Context

FITT is a web-first, API-first application intended to support future clients such as iOS. The backend must remain clean, understandable, and extensible while being feasible for a solo developer.

Early design decisions should avoid overly narrow domains that block future growth, while still keeping v1 focused and simple.

## Module Definitions

### Identity

Owns:
- User accounts
- Authentication and authorization
- Profile-related data (non-fitness)

Does not own:
- Fitness metrics
- Workouts
- Nutrition logic

### Workouts

Owns:
- Workout programs and routines
- Exercise selections
- Set, rep, and scheme definitions
- Progressive overload structure

Does not own:
- User identity
- Body measurements
- Nutrition calculations

### Measurements

Owns:
- Weight logs (v1)
- Historical measurement tracking
- Time-based measurement history

Future extensions may include:
- Body fat percentage
- Circumference measurements
- Performance metrics such as RPE

Does not own:
- Workout definitions
- Nutrition logic

### Nutrition

Owns:
- Calorie targets and recommendations
- Goal-based calorie logic (cut, maintain, bulk)

Does not own:
- Food databases
- Barcode scanning
- Meal-level tracking

## Dependency Rules

- Identity has no dependency on other modules
- Workouts may depend on Identity for user ownership
- Measurements may depend on Identity for user ownership
- Nutrition may depend on Identity and Measurements
- No module may directly access another module’s persistence layer

## Consequences

This structure:
- Keeps responsibilities clear
- Allows future expansion without breaking v1
- Prevents god services and cross-module coupling
- Supports long-term bodybuilding and powerlifting features such as RPE without forcing them into v1

The tradeoff is that discipline is required to maintain boundaries as the codebase grows.

# ADR-0003: V1 Domain Models Approved

Status: Accepted  
Date: 2025-12-24

## Decision

I have completed and approved the v1 domain model diagrams for FITT. These diagrams define the core entities, attributes, and relationships for version 1 across the four domains:

- Identity
- Workouts
- Measurements
- Nutrition

These diagrams will be treated as the source of truth for initial entity design and will guide implementation of JPA entities, DTOs, and REST endpoints.

## Scope

The diagrams capture domain concepts and relationships, not database schema or UI design.

The diagrams intentionally exclude:
- Food database and barcode scanning
- Social features
- Medical or nutritional coaching liability
- Advanced powerlifting/bodybuilding features beyond initial RPE placement

- domain-identity
- domain-workouts
- domain-measurements
- domain-nutrition

## Consequences

If future features require structural changes, I will update the diagrams and create an ADR documenting the change before modifying core entities.

FILE: docs/api/phase-5-workouts-api.md

# Phase 5: Workouts API Contract v1

This file is the contract for the Workouts endpoints. Controllers must match this behavior exactly so the frontend can integrate without guessing. Internals can evolve later, but this contract stays stable unless I explicitly version it.

## Auth and ownership rules

- All `/api/workouts/**` endpoints require authentication.
- Ownership-safe behavior is mandatory:
- If a workout does not exist OR it exists but belongs to a different user, return `404 Not Found`.
- Do not return `403` for “not owned” because that confirms the resource exists.

## Content types

- Requests: `Content-Type: application/json`
- Responses: `Content-Type: application/json` (except 204)

## Public DTOs

CreateWorkoutRequest
- `name` string, required, must not be blank

WorkoutResponse
- `id` integer
- `name` string
- `createdAt` ISO-8601 timestamp string
- `updatedAt` ISO-8601 timestamp string

Error format (Problem Details, RFC 9457 style)
- We return one consistent error shape everywhere.
- Fields:
- `type` string (URI), optional but preferred
- `title` string
- `status` integer
- `detail` string
- `instance` string (URI), optional

## Endpoints

### POST /api/workouts

What it does
- Creates a workout owned by the authenticated user.

Request body
- CreateWorkoutRequest

Example body
- `{ "name": "Push Day" }`

Success
- `201 Created`
- Response body is the created WorkoutResponse

Validation errors
- `400 Bad Request`
- Problem Details payload (example cases: missing name, blank name)

### GET /api/workouts/{workoutId}

What it does
- Returns one workout by id, but only if it belongs to the authenticated user.

Path param
- `workoutId` integer, required

Success
- `200 OK`
- WorkoutResponse

Not found / not owned
- `404 Not Found` (ownership-safe)

### DELETE /api/workouts/{workoutId}

What it does
- Deletes one workout by id, but only if it belongs to the authenticated user.

Path param
- `workoutId` integer, required

Success
- `204 No Content`
- No response body

Not found / not owned
- `404 Not Found` (ownership-safe)

## Implementation notes (non-negotiable)

- Controllers do not return entities directly.
- Controllers map request DTO -> service call -> response DTO.
- Errors are uniform Problem Details (no random `{ "error": "..." }` shapes).

# FITT Architecture (C4)

We will use two C4 diagrams to describe FITT at the start:
- System Context
- Container

C4 is a lightweight way to describe software architecture using a consistent set of diagram types and abstractions.

## System Context, what exists

Purpose
Show the system boundary. Who uses FITT and what external systems it depends on.

Actors
- End user (lifter)

Software systems
- FITT (the system)
- Database (local in development, hosted in production later)

Future systems (not v1)
- Messaging or sharing services
- Cloud hosting and remote sync
- iOS client using the same backend API

Draw.io instructions
Create a diagram with two boxes and one person:
- Person: End user
- Box: FITT
Connect End user -> FITT with “uses”

Optionally annotate that FITT stores data in a database, but keep it high level.

## Container view (how it runs)

Purpose
Show the runtime pieces that make FITT work and how they communicate.

Containers
- Web client (browser UI)
- Backend API (rules, auth, persistence orchestration)
- Database (source of truth for user data)

Trust boundaries
- Browser client is untrusted
- API is the enforcement boundary
- Database is private to the API

Draw.io instructions
Create three boxes and one person:
- Person: End user
- Box: Web client
- Box: Backend API
- Cylinder: Database

Connections
- End user -> Web client “uses”
- Web client -> Backend API “HTTPS/JSON”
- Backend API -> Database “SQL”

Diagram checklist
Before you consider the diagram done, verify that:
- Every box has a clear responsibility
- The database is not connected directly to the user
- The API is the boundary where validation and authorization live

# FITT — Sprint 0 Blueprint
Status: Approved
Last updated: 2025-12-23

This document explains why FITT exists, who it is for, what success means, what is out of scope for v1, and when the project should stop. It is the foundation for the architecture and repo setup that comes next.

## Why this project exists

There is a gap in the fitness app space for people who lift weights and want a simple, budget-friendly tool that supports real training progress. Many apps are expensive, noisy, or bloated. Users end up tracking in journals, guessing calories, or relying on memory. That makes training harder than it needs to be and can slow progress.

This project exists because that pain shows up daily for lifters, and the founder is also a user with the same problem.

## Who this is for

Primary user
A person who trains with intention. This includes bodybuilders, powerlifters, and anyone serious about tracking workouts and progress.

Not the user
People who do not care about training, diet, or tracking progress.

Context and constraints
The problem appears when the user forgets what they did last session, cannot track progressive overload cleanly, or feels unsure about calories and goals. Common constraints are attention, memory, consistency, and knowledge.

## What success looks like

If FITT succeeds, the user feels confident that their training and diet choices are reasonable. It becomes easier to answer questions like surplus vs deficit and how progressive overload applies in practice.

Success is measurable
Strength increases over time, weight trends move in the intended direction, and physique improves. The user can look back and see proof of progress.

## What v1 will not do

v1 is intentionally limited. It will not include:
- A MyFitnessPal-style food database or barcode scanning
- Social features like friends, sharing, feeds, or messaging
- Medical advice, clinical nutrition guidance, or coaching liability

These boundaries exist to prevent a half-built product and to avoid security and quality shortcuts.

## Project shape and constraints

This is both a learning project and a real tool I intend to use. If it proves useful, it may become portfolio-ready and later public or commercial.

Current constraints include time, money, and developing full-stack and mobile skills. Infrastructure should remain simple.

Reliability expectation for v1
Hobby-grade is acceptable, but the system must persist data. Workout history should not be casually lost. A real database is required, even if it is local in early stages.

Platform direction
Long term, the goal is iOS. v1 will be web-first to maximize learning and interview readiness, while keeping the API reusable for a future iOS client.

## Data and responsibility

Data handled includes:
- Name, date of birth, age, email, password
- Optional phone for 2FA, locale
- Fitness metrics, goals, workout history

Most sensitive data
Passwords and identifiers. Payment information would be highly sensitive if added later.

Accuracy expectations
Age, height, goals, and calories must be accurate for recommendations to be meaningful. Some estimates (like daily calorie expenditure) can be approximate.

Responsibility model
The system provides suggestions and structure. The user is responsible for applying it safely and consistently.

## Trust, ethics, and limits

Risks
Users may over-trust the system or assume results are automatic without discipline.

Boundaries
The app must present recommendations as suggestions and avoid claiming medical or nutritional authority. It is not a doctor, nutritionist, or personal coach.

## Stop conditions

Stop or pause if:
- Users are consistently unhappy, stability is poor, or reviews are overwhelmingly negative
- A security breach occurs that undermines trust
- The project does not reach a minimally functional state

It is irresponsible to charge users if promises are not met or if the product is unreliable.

## Deferred vision (not v1)

Future capabilities that are explicitly deferred:
- Barcode scanning and food databases
- Exercise demonstration media
- Onboarding maintenance-calorie estimation and recalculation flows
- Custom templates, default workouts, and recommended weights/sets/reps
- RPE and advanced bodybuilding/powerlifting tracking needs
- Social features

These are recorded to preserve the vision without letting v1 collapse under scope.

# FITT Docs

This repo starts with docs on purpose. The goal is to make decisions before code so the system stays focused and maintainable.

How to use this docs folder
Read in this order:
1) docs/blueprint/S0-blueprint.md
2) docs/architecture/C4-context-and-container.md
3) docs/adr/ (as decisions are made)

What each folder means
- docs/blueprint
  The project justification and v1 boundaries. This is the what and why.

- docs/architecture
  Lightweight architecture communication. I use C4 System Context and Container views to describe the system shape.
- docs/adr
  Decision log for architecturally significant decisions. ADRs keep “why we chose this” attached to the repo so decisions do not get lost. 

- docs/security
  Threat modeling notes and a baseline security checklist aligned to OWASP ASVS.

- docs/api
  API-first contract sketches. The web client and future iOS client should rely on stable contracts.

- docs/ops
  How we work. Definition of Done, testing approach, basic observability expectations.

Rule for this repo
If a decision changes the system shape, write an ADR before changing code.

import { inject } from '@angular/core';
import { CanActivateFn, Router } from '@angular/router';
import { AuthService } from '../services/auth.service';

export const authGuard: CanActivateFn = () => {
  const authService = inject(AuthService);
  const router = inject(Router);

  if (authService.isLoggedIn()) {
    return true;
  }

  return router.createUrlTree(['/login']);
};

FILE: frontend/src/app/core/interceptors/auth.interceptor.ts
================================================================================
import { HttpInterceptorFn } from '@angular/common/http';
import { inject } from '@angular/core';
import { AuthService } from '../services/auth.service';

// Adds the JWT and a unique request ID to every outgoing request.
// Angular HTTP requests are immutable so we clone before modifying.
export const authInterceptor: HttpInterceptorFn = (req, next) => {
  const authService = inject(AuthService);
  const token = authService.getToken();
  const requestId = crypto.randomUUID();

  const headers: Record<string, string> = {
    'X-Request-ID': requestId
  };

  if (token) {
    headers['Authorization'] = `Bearer ${token}`;
  }

  const augmentedReq = req.clone({ setHeaders: headers });
  return next(augmentedReq);
};

FILE: frontend/src/app/core/services/auth.service.ts
================================================================================
import { Injectable, signal } from '@angular/core';
import { HttpClient } from '@angular/common/http';
import { Observable, tap } from 'rxjs';

interface LoginRequest {
  username: string;
  password: string;
}

interface TokenResponse {
  token: string;
}

@Injectable({ providedIn: 'root' })
export class AuthService {

  private readonly TOKEN_KEY = 'fitt_token';

  // Signal exposes auth state reactively — guards and components
  // react automatically without manual subscriptions.
  isLoggedIn = signal<boolean>(this.hasToken());

  constructor(private http: HttpClient) {}

  login(username: string, password: string): Observable<TokenResponse> {
    return this.http.post<TokenResponse>(
      `/api/identity/auth/login`,
      { username, password } as LoginRequest
    ).pipe(
      // tap() stores the token as a side effect without altering
      // the emitted value the caller receives.
      tap(response => {
        localStorage.setItem(this.TOKEN_KEY, response.token);
        this.isLoggedIn.set(true);
      })
    );
  }

  logout(): void {
    localStorage.removeItem(this.TOKEN_KEY);
    this.isLoggedIn.set(false);
  }

  getToken(): string | null {
    return localStorage.getItem(this.TOKEN_KEY);
  }

  private hasToken(): boolean {
    return !!localStorage.getItem(this.TOKEN_KEY);
  }
}

FILE: frontend/src/app/core/services/workout.service.ts
================================================================================
import { Injectable } from '@angular/core';
import { HttpClient } from '@angular/common/http';
import { Observable } from 'rxjs';
import { Workout } from '../../features/workouts/models/workout.model';

@Injectable({ providedIn: 'root' })
export class WorkoutService {

  constructor(private http: HttpClient) {}

  getWorkouts(userId: number): Observable<Workout[]> {
    return this.http.get<Workout[]>(`/api/users/${userId}/workouts`);
  }

  createWorkout(userId: number, name: string): Observable<Workout> {
    return this.http.post<Workout>(`/api/users/${userId}/workouts`, { name });
  }

  getWorkout(userId: number, workoutId: number): Observable<Workout> {
    return this.http.get<Workout>(`/api/users/${userId}/workouts/${workoutId}`);
  }

  deleteWorkout(userId: number, workoutId: number): Observable<void> {
    return this.http.delete<void>(`/api/users/${userId}/workouts/${workoutId}`);
  }
}

import { Component } from '@angular/core';
import { FormsModule } from '@angular/forms';
import { Router } from '@angular/router';
import { AuthService } from '../../../core/services/auth.service';

@Component({
  selector: 'app-login',
  standalone: true,
  imports: [FormsModule],
  templateUrl: './login.html',
  styleUrl: './login.scss'
})
export class LoginComponent {

  username = '';
  password = '';
  errorMessage = '';
  loading = false;

  constructor(
    private authService: AuthService,
    private router: Router
  ) {}

  onSubmit(): void {
    this.loading = true;
    this.errorMessage = '';

    this.authService.login(this.username, this.password).subscribe({
      next: () => {
        this.router.navigate(['/workouts']);
      },
      error: () => {
        this.errorMessage = 'Invalid username or password.';
        this.loading = false;
      }
    });
  }
}

FILE: frontend/src/app/features/workouts/components/workouts.ts
================================================================================
import { Component, OnInit } from '@angular/core';
import { FormsModule } from '@angular/forms';
import { WorkoutService } from '../../../core/services/workout.service';
import { WorkoutCardComponent } from './workout-card';
import { Workout } from '../models/workout.model';

@Component({
  selector: 'app-workouts',
  standalone: true,
  imports: [FormsModule, WorkoutCardComponent],
  templateUrl: './workouts.html',
  styleUrl: './workouts.scss'
})
export class WorkoutsComponent implements OnInit {

  private readonly userId = 1;

  workouts: Workout[] = [];
  newWorkoutName = '';
  errorMessage = '';
  loading = false;

  constructor(private workoutService: WorkoutService) {}

  ngOnInit(): void {
    this.loadWorkouts();
  }

  onCreateWorkout(): void {
    const name = this.newWorkoutName.trim();
    if (!name) return;

    this.workoutService.createWorkout(this.userId, name).subscribe({
      next: (created) => {
        this.workouts = [created, ...this.workouts];
        this.newWorkoutName = '';
      },
      error: () => {
        this.errorMessage = 'Failed to create workout.';
      }
    });
  }

  onDeleteWorkout(workoutId: number): void {
    this.workoutService.deleteWorkout(this.userId, workoutId).subscribe({
      next: () => {
        this.workouts = this.workouts.filter(w => w.id !== workoutId);
      },
      error: () => {
        this.errorMessage = 'Failed to delete workout.';
      }
    });
  }

  private loadWorkouts(): void {
    this.loading = true;
    this.workoutService.getWorkouts(this.userId).subscribe({
      next: (workouts) => {
        this.workouts = workouts;
        this.loading = false;
      },
      error: () => {
        this.errorMessage = 'Failed to load workouts.';
        this.loading = false;
      }
    });
  }
}

import { Routes } from '@angular/router';
import { authGuard } from './core/guards/auth.guard';
import { LoginComponent } from './features/auth/components/login';

export const routes: Routes = [
  {
    path: 'login',
    component: LoginComponent
  },
  {
    path: 'workouts',
    canActivate: [authGuard],
    loadComponent: () =>
      import('./features/workouts/components/workouts')
        .then(m => m.WorkoutsComponent)
  },
  {
    path: '',
    redirectTo: 'login',
    pathMatch: 'full'
  }
];

import { TestBed } from '@angular/core/testing';
import { App } from './app';

describe('App', () => {
  beforeEach(async () => {
    await TestBed.configureTestingModule({
      imports: [App],
    }).compileComponents();
  });

  it('should create the app', () => {
    const fixture = TestBed.createComponent(App);
    const app = fixture.componentInstance;
    expect(app).toBeTruthy();
  });

  it('should render title', async () => {
    const fixture = TestBed.createComponent(App);
    await fixture.whenStable();
    const compiled = fixture.nativeElement as HTMLElement;
    expect(compiled.querySelector('h1')?.textContent).toContain('Hello, fitt-web');
  });
});

# FittWeb

This project was generated using [Angular CLI](https://github.com/angular/angular-cli) version 21.0.4.

## Development server

To start a local development server, run:

```bash
ng serve
```

Once the server is running, open your browser and navigate to `http://localhost:4200/`. The application will automatically reload whenever you modify any of the source files.

## Code scaffolding

Angular CLI includes powerful code scaffolding tools. To generate a new component, run:

```bash
ng generate component component-name
```

For a complete list of available schematics (such as `components`, `directives`, or `pipes`), run:

```bash
ng generate --help
```

## Building

To build the project run:

```bash
ng build
```

This will compile your project and store the build artifacts in the `dist/` directory. By default, the production build optimizes your application for performance and speed.

## Running unit tests

To execute unit tests with the [Vitest](https://vitest.dev/) test runner, use the following command:

```bash
ng test
```

## Running end-to-end tests

For end-to-end (e2e) testing, run:

```bash
ng e2e
```

Angular CLI does not come with an end-to-end testing framework by default. You can choose one that suits your needs.

## Additional Resources

For more information on using the Angular CLI, including detailed command references, visit the [Angular CLI Overview and Command Reference](https://angular.dev/tools/cli) page.

userRepository,\n            PasswordEncoder passwordEncoder\n    ) {\n        this.authenticationManager = authenticationManager;\n        this.jwtEncoder = jwtEncoder;\n        this.jwtProperties =    // a DB constraint violation bubble up as a 500.\n    // Password is hashed before the entity is built so plain text never hits the DB.\n    public String register(String email, String password) {\n        if (userRepository.existsByEmail(email)) {\n            throw new EmailAlreadyExistsException(\"email already registered\");\n        }\n\n        String hash = passwordEncoder.encode(password);\n        UserEntity saved = userRepository.save(new UserEntity(email, hash));\n\n        return buildToken(saved);\n    }\n\n    // AuthenticationManager runs the     }\n\n        return buildToken(user);\n    }\n\n    // Shared by register and login so token structure has one place to change.\n    private String buildToken(UserEntity user) {\n        Instant .issuedAt(now)\n                .expiresAt(now.plusSeconds(jwtProperties.getTtlSeconds()))\n                .claim(\"uid\", user.getId())\n                .build();\n\n        JwsHeader header =       "content": "package com.fitt.shared.filter;\n\nimport jakarta.servlet.FilterChain;\nimport jakarta.servlet.ServletException;\nimport jakarta.servlet.http.HttpServletRequest;\nimport jakarta.servlet.http.HttpServletResponse;\nimport org.slf4j.MDC;\nimport org.jspecify.annotations.NonNull;\nimport org.springframework.stereotype.Component;\nimport org.springframework.web.filter.OncePerRequestFilter;\n\nimport java.io.IOException;\nimport java.util.UUID;\n\n// Stores the incoming X-Request-ID in the MDC so every log line produced\n// during this request automatically includes the correlation ID.\n// The ID is echoed in the response so callers can match client and server logs.\n@Component\npublic class CorrelationIdFilter extends OncePerRequestFilter {\n\n    private static final String REQUEST_ID_HEADER = \"X-Request-ID\";\n    private static final String MDC_KEY = \"requestId\";\n\n    @Override\n    protected void doFilterInternal(\n            @NonNull HttpServletRequest request,\n            @NonNull HttpServletResponse response,\n            @NonNull FilterChain filterChain\n    ) throws ServletException, IOException {\n\n        String requestId = request.getHeader(REQUEST_ID_HEADER);\n\n        if (requestId == null || requestId.isBlank()) {\n            requestId = UUID.randomUUID().toString();\n        }\n\n        MDC.put(MDC_KEY, requestId);\n        response.setHeader(REQUEST_ID_HEADER, requestId);\n\n        try {\n            filterChain.doFilter(request, response);\n        } finally {\n            // Tomcat reuses threads from a pool. Without clearing here, this\n            // requests correlation ID would appear in the next requests log lines.\n            MDC.clear();\n        }\n    }\n}",

const fs   = require('fs');
const path = require('path');

// directories to skip entirely
const EXCLUDE_DIRS = new Set([
    'node_modules', 'dist', 'build', 'coverage', '.angular',
    '.cache', '.idea', 'out', 'target', '.git', '.mvn', '.vscode'
]);

// file extensions to skip entirely
const EXCLUDE_EXTS = new Set([
    '.iml', '.log', '.class', '.jar', '.war', '.png', '.jpg',
    '.jpeg', '.gif', '.ico', '.svg', '.woff', '.woff2', '.ttf',
    '.eot', '.map', '.lock'
]);

// only dump contents for these extensions
const CONTENT_EXTS = new Set([
    '.java', '.ts', '.html', '.scss', '.css', '.json', '.xml',
    '.properties', '.yml', '.yaml', '.md', '.txt', '.http',
    '.sql', '.sh', '.js'
]);

const structureLines = [];
const contentLines   = [];

function dumpTree(dirPath, prefix = '') {
    let entries;
    try {
        entries = fs.readdirSync(dirPath, { withFileTypes: true });
    } catch {
        return;
    }

    entries = entries
        .filter(e => {
            if (e.isDirectory()) return !EXCLUDE_DIRS.has(e.name);
            return !EXCLUDE_EXTS.has(path.extname(e.name));
        })
        .sort((a, b) => {
            if (a.isDirectory() !== b.isDirectory()) return a.isDirectory() ? -1 : 1;
            return a.name.localeCompare(b.name);
        });

    entries.forEach((entry, i) => {
        const isLast    = i === entries.length - 1;
        const connector = isLast ? '└── ' : '├── ';
        const suffix    = entry.isDirectory() ? '/' : '';
        structureLines.push(`${prefix}${connector}${entry.name}${suffix}`);

        if (entry.isDirectory()) {
            const extension = isLast ? '    ' : '│   ';
            dumpTree(path.join(dirPath, entry.name), prefix + extension);
        }
    });
}

function dumpContents(dirPath) {
    let entries;
    try {
        entries = fs.readdirSync(dirPath, { withFileTypes: true });
    } catch {
        return;
    }

    entries
        .filter(e => {
            if (e.isDirectory()) return !EXCLUDE_DIRS.has(e.name);
            return !EXCLUDE_EXTS.has(path.extname(e.name));
        })
        .sort((a, b) => {
            if (a.isDirectory() !== b.isDirectory()) return a.isDirectory() ? -1 : 1;
            return a.name.localeCompare(b.name);
        })
        .forEach(entry => {
            const fullPath = path.join(dirPath, entry.name);
            if (entry.isDirectory()) {
                dumpContents(fullPath);
            } else if (CONTENT_EXTS.has(path.extname(entry.name))) {
                const relative = path.relative(process.cwd(), fullPath).replace(/\\/g, '/');
                contentLines.push('');
                contentLines.push('='.repeat(80));
                contentLines.push(`FILE: ${relative}`);
                contentLines.push('='.repeat(80));
                try {
                    const content = fs.readFileSync(fullPath, 'utf8');
                    contentLines.push(content);
                } catch {
                    contentLines.push('[could not read file]');
                }
            }
        });
}

const root = process.cwd();

// structure section
structureLines.push(path.basename(root) + '/');
dumpTree(root);

// contents section
dumpContents(root);

const output = [
    '='.repeat(80),
    'PROJECT STRUCTURE',
    '='.repeat(80),
    ...structureLines,
    '',
    '='.repeat(80),
    'FILE CONTENTS',
    '='.repeat(80),
    ...contentLines
].join('\n');

const outFile = path.join(root, 'project_dump.txt');
fs.writeFileSync(outFile, output, 'utf8');
console.log(`Done. project_dump.txt written to ${root}`);

# FITT

FITT is a full-stack fitness application built with Spring Boot and Angular.

The project is designed as a professional, portfolio-ready application with an emphasis on clean structure, clear separation of concerns, and real world development practices. 
It is built intentionally and incrementally.

---

## Tech Stack

Backend: Java, Spring Boot, Spring Data JPA
Frontend: Angular, TypeScript
Tooling: Maven, Node.js, npm, Git

---

## Repository Structure

This repository is organized as a monorepo.

The backend directory contains the Spring Boot application.  
The frontend directory contains the Angular application.

Each side of the stack is developed independently while sharing a single repository.

---

## Current Status

The project is under active development.

The backend application is bootstrapped and running. Core architecture and package structure are established, and domain modeling is in progress.

---

## Running the Project Locally

Backend:

From the `backend` directory, run:

`mvn spring-boot:run`

The backend starts on port 8080.

Frontend:

From the `frontend` directory, install dependencies and start the dev server:

`npm install`  
`ng serve`

The frontend starts on port 4200.

---

## Documentation

Project direction, development phases, and architectural decisions are documented in `roadmap.md`.

---

## Notes

This project is built with an emphasis on understanding design decisions and development workflow, not just producing features.

# FITT Project Roadmap

Spring Boot + Angular Full-Stack Application

## Purpose

The FITT project is a full-stack fitness application built as a professional learning and portfolio project.
The goal is not speed, shortcuts, or demo-level code. The goal is correct architecture, clear reasoning, and
industry-standard development practices.
Each phase builds intentionally on the previous one. Nothing is added early, and no layer exists without a clear reason.

---

## Product Definition (Approved 2026-03-11)

FITT is a fitness tracking application for people who train with intention. The primary user is a lifter who wants
to track workouts, monitor body weight trends, manage progressive overload, and understand their calorie goals.

### Screens and Features

**Authentication**
Login and sign up screen with two buttons. Login: credential entry. Sign up: email, password, confirm email,
then onboarding. MFA deferred to production.

**Onboarding (one-time, slideshow style)**
One question per screen with smooth transitions. Collects: height, current weight, date of birth, biological sex,
activity level, units preference (lbs/kg), goal direction (Bulk/Cut/Maintain), target weight (optional),
timeline, and calorie goal via TDEE calculation with auto/manual toggle.

**Main Screen**
Tab navigation: Weight Log / Workouts / Goals. Settings icon top right.
Body: session streak, 7-day average body weight, calorie goal, large CTA button for Today's Lift.

**Weight Log Tab**
Past 7 days of body weight with date in column format. Dropdown to expand to 30/60/90 days.
Daily reminder notification at user-set time. Prompt on app open if today not yet logged.

**Workouts Tab**
Active workout plan displayed in full (e.g. 16-week plan). Each day viewable and editable.
Dropdown to switch between saved plans with activate/delete options.
Create plan flow: days per week, day scheme (M-F/EOD/3-on-1-off/Custom),
split template (PPL/Upper-Lower/Full Body/Custom), exercise population from library.
Exercise library: fixed broad library by muscle group (Chest/Back/Shoulders/Arms/Legs/Glutes)
plus user-created custom exercises stored locally with edit and delete options.

**Active Session Screen**
Triggered by Today's Lift CTA. Global session timer from start.
Exercise rows with: exercise name, sets, reps, weight, RPE columns, per-row rest countdown timer.
After each set: green checkmark, row greys out, next row activates.
Finish button at bottom leads to workout summary: total volume, total time, PRs hit,
next session weight suggestions from progressive overload algorithm.
Progression model selectable by user with info icon explaining each model.

**Goals Tab**
Bulk/Cut/Maintain selection, target weight, timeline, auto/manual calorie goal toggle with info icon,
TDEE-based starter calorie recommendation, editable calorie goal.

**Settings**
Personal info, contact info, units preference, notification preferences, delete account.

### Platform
Web-first. Clean professional web UI designed for desktop and browser.
iOS gets its own native SwiftUI design in Phase 21 consuming the same API.

### Deferred (not v1)
Nutrition database and food logging, MFA, social features, barcode scanning.

---

## Phase 0 — Foundations (Complete)

This phase establishes a stable baseline before any real development begins.

The repository is structured as a monorepo containing both frontend and backend.
Git is initialized at the correct root and kept clean from the start. A Spring Boot application is created and verified
to start successfully. The test context loads without error.
The backend package structure is scaffolded but intentionally left empty to avoid premature design decisions.

Outcome: a clean, trusted starting point with no architectural debt.

---

## Phase 1 — Backend Architecture Design (Complete)

This phase focuses on design rather than implementation.

The backend follows a layered architecture with clear separation of concerns. Each layer has a defined role:
configuration, controllers, services, repositories, domain entities, and DTOs.
Communication boundaries are defined early so that responsibilities do not blur later. Naming conventions and package
layout are established up front, and Spring's component scanning behavior is fully understood.

Outcome: a clear mental model of how the backend is structured and why.

---

## Phase 2 — Domain Modeling (Complete, Locked)

The domain model forms the core of the application.

Business concepts are identified first and then translated into domain entities. Fields are chosen deliberately with
correct data types, nullability, and constraints. JPA annotations are introduced carefully and explained in detail,
including entity identity, lifecycle, and persistence context. At this stage, repositories and services are
intentionally avoided to keep focus on the model itself.

Outcome: a solid understanding of what JPA entities represent and how they behave at runtime.

---

## Phase 3 — Data Access Layer (Complete, Locked)

This phase introduces persistence in a controlled way.

Spring Data JPA is added, and repositories are created for the domain entities. The difference between repositories and
traditional DAOs is explained. Query method naming conventions are covered, along with basic transaction concepts. Lazy
versus eager loading is introduced with attention to real-world consequences.

Outcome: a clear understanding of how data is stored, retrieved, and managed.

---

## Phase 4 — Service Layer (Complete)

This phase introduces application behavior.

Services are used to coordinate business logic rather than acting as dumping grounds. Controllers remain thin, and
persistence concerns remain in repositories. Transactional boundaries are introduced where appropriate. Validation logic
is separated from persistence, and DTO mapping is handled explicitly rather than hidden behind magic.

Outcome: business logic that is readable, testable, and maintainable.

---

## Phase 5 — Controllers and API Design (Complete)

This phase exposes functionality through stable APIs.

REST principles are applied consistently. Endpoints are named intentionally, and HTTP methods are used correctly.
Request and response DTOs are kept separate. Validation, error handling, and status codes are handled in a predictable
and professional way.

Outcome: APIs that look and behave like real production systems.

---

## Phase 6 — Backend Security (Complete)

Security is designed into the system rather than added later.

Authentication and authorization are clearly separated. JWT concepts are introduced, along with Spring Security's
architecture and filter chain. Endpoints are protected intentionally, and the backend is kept stateless.
Object-level authorization enforced on all user-scoped resources.

Outcome: a secure backend with a clear security model.

---

## Phase 7 — Frontend Foundations (Complete)

This phase establishes Angular fundamentals.

Angular architecture is explained from first principles. The purpose of TypeScript is made clear. Components, services,
and modules each have defined roles. The Angular CLI and build process are understood rather than treated as black
boxes. Environment configuration is handled properly. Auth service, JWT interceptor, and route guard implemented.

Outcome: Angular becomes predictable rather than confusing.

---

## Phase 8 — Frontend Feature Development (Complete)

This phase focused on real user-facing functionality with a workouts placeholder implementation.

Routing and guards introduced. HTTP client integrated with the backend. Observable-based data flow implemented.
Workouts list, create, and delete wired end-to-end against the Spring backend with JWT authentication.

Outcome: a frontend that communicates correctly with the backend.

---

## Phase 9 — Full-Stack Integration

This phase connects frontend and backend into a single system and prepares the infrastructure for all future phases.

CORS is explained and configured correctly on the backend. API proxying confirmed as development-only.
Environment separation enforced. Correlation ID tracing implemented across Angular interceptor and Spring filter.
End-to-end request tracing verified across layers.

Outcome: the ability to reason about the entire system as one unit.

---

## Phase 10 — Domain Expansion: Identity and Onboarding

Real user registration replaces the hardcoded uid=1L placeholder throughout the system.

User registration endpoint, biometrics entity, goals entity, TDEE calculation service, and onboarding API.
UserEntity introduced with proper identity management. JWT uid claim wired to real database user IDs.
All ownership enforcement updated to use real principal identifiers.

Outcome: real multi-user identity with secure, user-scoped data access.

---

## Phase 11 — Domain Expansion: Workouts Full Implementation

The Workout placeholder is replaced with the full domain model from Phase 2.

WorkoutSession, ExerciseEntry, and SetEntry hierarchy implemented in full. Workout plan entity with split templates.
Exercise library with fixed entries by muscle group. Custom exercise support. Full backend: entities, repositories,
services, controllers, and ownership enforcement at every level.

Outcome: a complete, production-grade workouts domain.

---

## Phase 12 — Domain Expansion: Measurements

Body weight logging introduced as a first-class domain.

BodyWeightEntry entity, daily logging endpoint, 7-day average calculation service.
Historical query support for 30/60/90 day views. Ownership enforced.

Outcome: a complete measurements domain ready for frontend integration.

---

## Phase 13 — Progressive Overload Algorithm

Science-backed progression logic implemented as a backend service.

Literature review: double progression, RPE-based autoregulation, linear periodization.
Selectable progression model per user. Post-session analysis generates next session weight suggestions.
Algorithm service designed for extensibility as more models are added.

Outcome: a defensible, evidence-based progression engine.

---

## Phase 14 — Frontend Rebuild: Authentication and Onboarding

Login and sign up screens rebuilt to production quality.

Slideshow onboarding flow wired to Phase 10 backend. Units preference, biometrics, goals, TDEE display.
Smooth screen transitions. Form validation and error handling at every step.

Outcome: a complete, polished authentication and onboarding experience.

---

## Phase 15 — Frontend Rebuild: Main Screen and Navigation

Tab navigation shell established as the permanent application frame.

Main screen: session streak, 7-day weight average, calorie goal, Today's Lift CTA fully wired to backend.
Settings screen: personal info, contact info, units, notifications, delete account.

Outcome: a fully navigable application shell.

---

## Phase 16 — Frontend Rebuild: Workouts

Full workout plan builder UI with all active session features.

Exercise library with muscle group sections and custom exercise management.
Active session screen: global timer, per-row rest timer, set logging, green checkmark flow,
Finish button, workout summary screen with volume, time, PRs, and next session suggestions.
Date navigator (MyFitnessPal style) for session history.

Outcome: the core product feature, fully functional and polished.

---

## Phase 17 — Frontend Rebuild: Weight Log and Goals

Weight log tab with 7/30/60/90 day views and daily prompt on app open.
Goals tab: Bulk/Cut/Maintain, target weight, timeline, TDEE calorie goal, auto/manual toggle with info icons.

Outcome: all remaining product screens complete.

---

## Phase 18 — Testing Strategy

Testing introduced as a tool for confidence, not ceremony.

Unit and integration testing across all domains. Testcontainers for database-backed integration tests.
Frontend component testing. Decisions made about what should and should not be tested.

Outcome: tests that add value rather than friction.

---

## Phase 19 — Build, Docker, and Deployment

This phase focuses on delivery.

Maven lifecycle revisited. Docker fundamentals explained including image creation and container behavior.
Environment variables handled correctly. Production CORS locked to deployed frontend URL.
Differences between local and cloud environments understood.

Outcome: a clear understanding of how software leaves the development machine.

---

## Phase 20 — Polish and Portfolio Readiness

This phase prepares the project for external review.

Codebase reviewed for quality and clarity. Dead code removed. Naming improved.

Project prepared to be explained confidently in interviews.

Outcome: a portfolio-ready project that can be defended technically and verbally.

---

## Phase 21 — Mobile (iOS)

Native iOS client consuming the same backend API.

SwiftUI native design for mobile form factor. Workout logging, weight log, goals, and onboarding.

# FITT

FITT is a full-stack fitness application built with Spring Boot and Angular.

The project is designed as a professional, portfolio-ready application with an emphasis on clean structure, clear separation of concerns, and real world development practices. 
It is built intentionally and incrementally.

---

## Tech Stack

Backend: Java, Spring Boot, Spring Data JPA
Frontend: Angular, TypeScript
Tooling: Maven, Node.js, npm, Git

---

## Repository Structure

This repository is organized as a monorepo.

The backend directory contains the Spring Boot application.  
The frontend directory contains the Angular application.

Each side of the stack is developed independently while sharing a single repository.

---

## Current Status

The project is under active development.

The backend application is bootstrapped and running. Core architecture and package structure are established, and domain modeling is in progress.

---

## Running the Project Locally

Backend:

From the `backend` directory, run:

`mvn spring-boot:run`

The backend starts on port 8080.

Frontend:

From the `frontend` directory, install dependencies and start the dev server:

`npm install`  
`ng serve`

The frontend starts on port 4200.

---

## Documentation

Project direction, development phases, and architectural decisions are documented in `roadmap.md`.

---

## Notes

This project is built with an emphasis on understanding design decisions and development workflow, not just producing features.

# FITT Project Roadmap

Spring Boot + Angular Full-Stack Application

## Purpose

The FITT project is a full-stack fitness application built as a professional learning and portfolio project.
The goal is not speed, shortcuts, or demo-level code. The goal is correct architecture, clear reasoning, and
industry-standard development practices.
Each phase builds intentionally on the previous one. Nothing is added early, and no layer exists without a clear reason.

---

## Product Definition (Approved 2026-03-11)

FITT is a fitness tracking application for people who train with intention. The primary user is a lifter who wants
to track workouts, monitor body weight trends, manage progressive overload, and understand their calorie goals.

### Screens and Features

**Authentication**
Login and sign up screen with two buttons. Login: credential entry. Sign up: email, password, confirm email,
then onboarding. MFA deferred to production.

**Onboarding (one-time, slideshow style)**
One question per screen with smooth transitions. Collects: height, current weight, date of birth, biological sex,
activity level, units preference (lbs/kg), goal direction (Bulk/Cut/Maintain), target weight (optional),
timeline, and calorie goal via TDEE calculation with auto/manual toggle.

**Main Screen**
Tab navigation: Weight Log / Workouts / Goals. Settings icon top right.
Body: session streak, 7-day average body weight, calorie goal, large CTA button for Today's Lift.

**Weight Log Tab**
Past 7 days of body weight with date in column format. Dropdown to expand to 30/60/90 days.
Daily reminder notification at user-set time. Prompt on app open if today not yet logged.

**Workouts Tab**
Active workout plan displayed in full (e.g. 16-week plan). Each day viewable and editable.
Dropdown to switch between saved plans with activate/delete options.
Create plan flow: days per week, day scheme (M-F/EOD/3-on-1-off/Custom),
split template (PPL/Upper-Lower/Full Body/Custom), exercise population from library.
Exercise library: fixed broad library by muscle group (Chest/Back/Shoulders/Arms/Legs/Glutes)
plus user-created custom exercises stored locally with edit and delete options.

**Active Session Screen**
Triggered by Today's Lift CTA. Global session timer from start.
Exercise rows with: exercise name, sets, reps, weight, RPE columns, per-row rest countdown timer.
After each set: green checkmark, row greys out, next row activates.
Finish button at bottom leads to workout summary: total volume, total time, PRs hit,
next session weight suggestions from progressive overload algorithm.
Progression model selectable by user with info icon explaining each model.

**Goals Tab**
Bulk/Cut/Maintain selection, target weight, timeline, auto/manual calorie goal toggle with info icon,
TDEE-based starter calorie recommendation, editable calorie goal.

**Settings**
Personal info, contact info, units preference, notification preferences, delete account.

### Platform
Web-first. Clean professional web UI designed for desktop and browser.
iOS gets its own native SwiftUI design in Phase 21 consuming the same API.

### Deferred (not v1)
Nutrition database and food logging, MFA, social features, barcode scanning.

---

## Phase 0 — Foundations (Complete)

This phase establishes a stable baseline before any real development begins.

The repository is structured as a monorepo containing both frontend and backend.
Git is initialized at the correct root and kept clean from the start. A Spring Boot application is created and verified
to start successfully. The test context loads without error.
The backend package structure is scaffolded but intentionally left empty to avoid premature design decisions.

Outcome: a clean, trusted starting point with no architectural debt.

---

## Phase 1 — Backend Architecture Design (Complete)

This phase focuses on design rather than implementation.

The backend follows a layered architecture with clear separation of concerns. Each layer has a defined role:
configuration, controllers, services, repositories, domain entities, and DTOs.
Communication boundaries are defined early so that responsibilities do not blur later. Naming conventions and package
layout are established up front, and Spring's component scanning behavior is fully understood.

Outcome: a clear mental model of how the backend is structured and why.

---

## Phase 2 — Domain Modeling (Complete, Locked)

The domain model forms the core of the application.

Business concepts are identified first and then translated into domain entities. Fields are chosen deliberately with
correct data types, nullability, and constraints. JPA annotations are introduced carefully and explained in detail,
including entity identity, lifecycle, and persistence context. At this stage, repositories and services are
intentionally avoided to keep focus on the model itself.

Outcome: a solid understanding of what JPA entities represent and how they behave at runtime.

---

## Phase 3 — Data Access Layer (Complete, Locked)

This phase introduces persistence in a controlled way.

Spring Data JPA is added, and repositories are created for the domain entities. The difference between repositories and
traditional DAOs is explained. Query method naming conventions are covered, along with basic transaction concepts. Lazy
versus eager loading is introduced with attention to real-world consequences.

Outcome: a clear understanding of how data is stored, retrieved, and managed.

---

## Phase 4 — Service Layer (Complete)

This phase introduces application behavior.

Services are used to coordinate business logic rather than acting as dumping grounds. Controllers remain thin, and
persistence concerns remain in repositories. Transactional boundaries are introduced where appropriate. Validation logic
is separated from persistence, and DTO mapping is handled explicitly rather than hidden behind magic.

Outcome: business logic that is readable, testable, and maintainable.

---

## Phase 5 — Controllers and API Design (Complete)

This phase exposes functionality through stable APIs.

REST principles are applied consistently. Endpoints are named intentionally, and HTTP methods are used correctly.
Request and response DTOs are kept separate. Validation, error handling, and status codes are handled in a predictable
and professional way.

Outcome: APIs that look and behave like real production systems.

---

## Phase 6 — Backend Security (Complete)

Security is designed into the system rather than added later.

Authentication and authorization are clearly separated. JWT concepts are introduced, along with Spring Security's
architecture and filter chain. Endpoints are protected intentionally, and the backend is kept stateless.
Object-level authorization enforced on all user-scoped resources.

Outcome: a secure backend with a clear security model.

---

## Phase 7 — Frontend Foundations (Complete)

This phase establishes Angular fundamentals.

Angular architecture is explained from first principles. The purpose of TypeScript is made clear. Components, services,
and modules each have defined roles. The Angular CLI and build process are understood rather than treated as black
boxes. Environment configuration is handled properly. Auth service, JWT interceptor, and route guard implemented.

Outcome: Angular becomes predictable rather than confusing.

---

## Phase 8 — Frontend Feature Development (Complete)

This phase focused on real user-facing functionality with a workouts placeholder implementation.

Routing and guards introduced. HTTP client integrated with the backend. Observable-based data flow implemented.
Workouts list, create, and delete wired end-to-end against the Spring backend with JWT authentication.

Outcome: a frontend that communicates correctly with the backend.

---

## Phase 9 — Full-Stack Integration

This phase connects frontend and backend into a single system and prepares the infrastructure for all future phases.

CORS is explained and configured correctly on the backend. API proxying confirmed as development-only.
Environment separation enforced. Correlation ID tracing implemented across Angular interceptor and Spring filter.
End-to-end request tracing verified across layers.

Outcome: the ability to reason about the entire system as one unit.

---

## Phase 10 — Domain Expansion: Identity and Onboarding

Real user registration replaces the hardcoded uid=1L placeholder throughout the system.

User registration endpoint, biometrics entity, goals entity, TDEE calculation service, and onboarding API.
UserEntity introduced with proper identity management. JWT uid claim wired to real database user IDs.
All ownership enforcement updated to use real principal identifiers.

Outcome: real multi-user identity with secure, user-scoped data access.

---

## Phase 11 — Domain Expansion: Workouts Full Implementation

The Workout placeholder is replaced with the full domain model from Phase 2.

WorkoutSession, ExerciseEntry, and SetEntry hierarchy implemented in full. Workout plan entity with split templates.
Exercise library with fixed entries by muscle group. Custom exercise support. Full backend: entities, repositories,
services, controllers, and ownership enforcement at every level.

Outcome: a complete, production-grade workouts domain.

---

## Phase 12 — Domain Expansion: Measurements

Body weight logging introduced as a first-class domain.

BodyWeightEntry entity, daily logging endpoint, 7-day average calculation service.
Historical query support for 30/60/90 day views. Ownership enforced.

Outcome: a complete measurements domain ready for frontend integration.

---

## Phase 13 — Progressive Overload Algorithm

Science-backed progression logic implemented as a backend service.

Literature review: double progression, RPE-based autoregulation, linear periodization.
Selectable progression model per user. Post-session analysis generates next session weight suggestions.
Algorithm service designed for extensibility as more models are added.

Outcome: a defensible, evidence-based progression engine.

---

## Phase 14 — Frontend Rebuild: Authentication and Onboarding

Login and sign up screens rebuilt to production quality.

Slideshow onboarding flow wired to Phase 10 backend. Units preference, biometrics, goals, TDEE display.
Smooth screen transitions. Form validation and error handling at every step.

Outcome: a complete, polished authentication and onboarding experience.

---

## Phase 15 — Frontend Rebuild: Main Screen and Navigation

Tab navigation shell established as the permanent application frame.

Main screen: session streak, 7-day weight average, calorie goal, Today's Lift CTA fully wired to backend.
Settings screen: personal info, contact info, units, notifications, delete account.

Outcome: a fully navigable application shell.

---

## Phase 16 — Frontend Rebuild: Workouts

Full workout plan builder UI with all active session features.

Exercise library with muscle group sections and custom exercise management.
Active session screen: global timer, per-row rest timer, set logging, green checkmark flow,
Finish button, workout summary screen with volume, time, PRs, and next session suggestions.
Date navigator (MyFitnessPal style) for session history.

Outcome: the core product feature, fully functional and polished.

---

## Phase 17 — Frontend Rebuild: Weight Log and Goals

Weight log tab with 7/30/60/90 day views and daily prompt on app open.
Goals tab: Bulk/Cut/Maintain, target weight, timeline, TDEE calorie goal, auto/manual toggle with info icons.

Outcome: all remaining product screens complete.

---

## Phase 18 — Testing Strategy

Testing introduced as a tool for confidence, not ceremony.

Unit and integration testing across all domains. Testcontainers for database-backed integration tests.
Frontend component testing. Decisions made about what should and should not be tested.

Outcome: tests that add value rather than friction.

---

## Phase 19 — Build, Docker, and Deployment

This phase focuses on delivery.

Maven lifecycle revisited. Docker fundamentals explained including image creation and container behavior.
Environment variables handled correctly. Production CORS locked to deployed frontend URL.
Differences between local and cloud environments understood.

Outcome: a clear understanding of how software leaves the development machine.

---

## Phase 20 — Polish and Portfolio Readiness

This phase prepares the project for external review.

Codebase reviewed for quality and clarity. Dead code removed. Naming improved.
Architectural decisions documented. Study guide produced covering the full stack.
Project prepared to be explained confidently in interviews.

Outcome: a portfolio-ready project that can be defended technically and verbally.

---

## Phase 21 — Mobile (iOS)

Native iOS client consuming the same backend API.

SwiftUI native design for mobile form factor. Workout logging, weight log, goals, and onboarding.
Secure API integration with JWT. Designed specifically for iOS interaction patterns.

Outcome: a native mobile client that demonstrates full-stack and mobile engineering capability.
